name: Data and AI knowledge graph
description: Spine-first knowledge graph covering data and AI from hardware to presentation. The spine is a strict three-level hierarchy: layer -> sub_domain -> topic. Everything that is not a containment relationship is expressed as a facet or an edge. Topics inherit facets from their sub_domain unless they declare their own.

rules: Every topic is something a person can learn and be tested on.
A parent aims for 4 to 9 children. Fewer suggests merging; more suggests splitting.
Tools never appear in the spine. They attach via implemented_by edges.
A topic has exactly one parent. All other relationships are edges.

lenses.mstr: Optional MicroStrategy lens, read against the modern spine. A layer may carry `mstr: {summary}`. A sub_domain or concern may carry `mstr: {where, name, note}`, where `where` is `inside` (a capability of the MicroStrategy platform itself), `beside` (the customer stack MicroStrategy sat on) or `none` (no counterpart; the default). A topic may carry a short `mstr` label naming its closest MicroStrategy object. The lens maps responsibilities; it does not claim that MicroStrategy contained the platform or that each feature has a replacement.

edge_types.requires: A cannot be understood or used without B.
edge_types.part_of: A is a component of B across the spine, not under it.
edge_types.implemented_by: A is realised by tool or product B.
edge_types.alternative_to: A and B solve the same problem differently.
edge_types.governed_by: A is constrained by cross-cutting concern B.

layers.name: Infrastructure and hardware
layers.summary: The physical and platform substrate everything else runs on.

mstr.summary: MicroStrategy ran on servers the customer provisioned and sized. Hardware, networking and runtime decisions were made outside the BI platform.

topics.name: Block, file and object storage interfaces

mstr.name: Intelligence Server sizing
mstr.note: Memory for cubes and caches, and the number of clustered nodes, were recurring capacity decisions made on customer-run servers.

layers.name: Storage and persistence
layers.summary: How bytes are laid out, described and durably kept.

mstr.summary: MicroStrategy sat on top of the customer's warehouse — Teradata, Oracle, Netezza and others — and kept its own metadata in a relational repository. Inside the server it held Intelligent Cubes and result caches.

topics.name: Raw, refined and curated zone layering

mstr.name: Metadata and statistics repositories
mstr.note: MicroStrategy's metadata repository and statistics tables lived in a relational database the customer operated.

mstr.name: Enterprise warehouse (Teradata · Oracle · Netezza)
mstr.note: The warehouse supplied the data and executed the generated SQL. Partitioning, aggregate tables and physical design shaped report performance — essential to every deployment, but not MicroStrategy capabilities. A semantic model cannot compensate indefinitely for unclear grain, unstable source data or a poor physical design.

topics.name: Materialized views and result reuse
topics.mstr: Aggregate tables chosen by the SQL Engine

topics.name: Index refresh, sizing and scale limits

mstr.name: Intelligent Cubes and result caches
mstr.note: Intelligent Cubes held prepared data in Intelligence Server memory, and Dynamic Sourcing let eligible reports answer from a cube instead of the warehouse. The design question is not “warehouse or cube” but which work to compute on demand, which to precompute, and how to keep the two answers consistent.

layers.name: Processing and movement
layers.summary: Getting data in, moving it, and reshaping it at scale.

mstr.summary: Data arrived through ETL the customer ran. Inside MicroStrategy, the SQL Engine turned report definitions into warehouse SQL, MultiSource reached across databases, and the Analytical Engine finished calculations in memory.

mstr.name: External ETL (Informatica · DataStage)
mstr.note: ETL commonly happened outside the BI platform, often as repeated full extracts or timestamp-based loads. Modern stacks make ingestion, transformation and orchestration explicit parts of the platform.

topics.name: Log-based brokers and the commit log

mstr.name: SQL Engine · Analytical Engine · MultiSource
mstr.note: Between a business question and a result is a planner. The SQL Engine chose join paths and fact tables, wrote multi-pass SQL for non-additive metrics and tuned SQL per database; the Analytical Engine finished subtotals, ranking and cross-tabs; MultiSource combined databases. The same responsibility now spreads across semantic compilers, BI query generators and database optimizers.

topics.name: Semantic SQL generation and multi-pass queries
topics.mstr: Multi-pass SQL from the SQL Engine

mstr.name: Warehouse views and logical views
mstr.note: Warehouse views and logical views shaped the data available to analytics. SQL models and data products make those transformations easier to version, test and deploy.

layers.name: Semantics and features
layers.summary: Where raw data acquires agreed meaning and becomes model input.

mstr.summary: The part of MicroStrategy that most strongly shapes the mental model: attributes, facts, metrics, filters, hierarchies and prompts formed one language for asking business questions, stored as objects in one metadata repository.

mstr.name: Attributes, facts and the logical data model
mstr.note: Attributes, forms, lookup tables and relationships defined business entities and drill paths; facts separated source values from business calculations.

mstr.name: Metrics, filters, prompts and hierarchies
mstr.note: Metrics, level metrics, transformations, filters, prompts, custom groups and hierarchies were reusable objects in one repository. The hardest cases are where a metric changes meaning with its grain, filter context or join path — judge a semantic layer by the questions it can express and explain.

layers.name: Intelligence
layers.summary: Building, adapting, running and applying models.

mstr.summary: MicroStrategy was a BI platform, not a model-building one. Data Mining Services could evaluate predictive models trained elsewhere as metrics; training, LLMs and retrieval sit outside its boundary.

mstr.name: Data Mining Services
mstr.note: Predictive models built in other tools could be imported (PMML) and evaluated as predictive metrics inside reports.

topics.name: When to tune versus prompt versus retrieve

layers.name: Serving and access
layers.summary: How data and model outputs are exposed to consumers.

mstr.summary: Intelligence Server was also the access layer: roles, ACLs and security filters governed objects and rows, and REST APIs and embedding exposed the same governed results to applications.

mstr.name: REST API
mstr.note: REST APIs exposed reports, cubes and dossiers to applications under the same metadata and security.

mstr.name: Embedded analytics
mstr.note: Embedding placed dossiers and reports inside other applications; semantic APIs and SQL endpoints now carry that job across tools.

mstr.name: Users, security roles, ACLs and security filters
mstr.note: Roles and ACLs governed objects; security filters restricted the rows each user could see — inside MicroStrategy's own boundary. Moving policy closer to the data broadens coverage to more consumers, but definitions, access rules and deployment must then agree across tools.

layers.name: Consumption and experience
layers.summary: Where people actually meet the data and the models.

mstr.summary: Reports, documents, dossiers and mobile apps were the primary destination for the semantic model, and Distribution Services delivered them on schedule. The same definitions now also need to reach APIs, alerts and AI interfaces.

mstr.name: Reports, documents and dossiers
mstr.note: Reports and documents carried the semantic model to people, and self-service users built dossiers from governed attributes and metrics.

mstr.name: Grids, graphs and dossier visualizations
mstr.note: Grids, graphs and visualizations rendered results from the same metadata objects.

mstr.name: Natural-language query
mstr.note: NLQ and contextual experiences needed what AI assistants still need: governed metrics, clear context and explainable queries.

mstr.name: Alerts, subscriptions and mobile
mstr.note: Threshold alerts, scheduled delivery and mobile apps pushed results into people's working day.

mstr.name: Schedules and Command Manager
mstr.note: Time- and event-based schedules refreshed caches, cubes and subscriptions, and Command Manager scripted administration. Data pipelines themselves were orchestrated outside, in the ETL tools.

mstr.name: One metadata repository
mstr.note: One repository made a large analytics estate feel like one connected object system: report-to-metric-to-attribute dependencies were inspectable. Modern stacks split physical metadata, business definitions, deployment history and lineage across several systems — can you still trace a changed column to every report, API and decision it affects?

mstr.name: Object ACLs and security filters
mstr.note: Policies lived on BI objects and results, within the server's boundary. Moving them closer to the data lets more consumers share the same rules.

mstr.name: Users, groups and authentication
mstr.note: Users, groups and authentication modes were administered inside the platform, often synchronized from LDAP or a single sign-on provider.

topics.name: Encryption at rest and in transit
Prompt injection, unsafe agency and model attacks

mstr.name: Integrity Manager and Platform Analytics
mstr.note: Report comparison caught changes in output between versions or environments, and platform analytics exposed adoption and performance. Data tests, data diffs, semantic validation and dashboard checks now cover different parts of that risk.

mstr.name: Clustering and governing settings
mstr.note: Clustered Intelligence Servers and governing settings controlled analytics demand and failover; compute platforms and query engines now manage concurrency, resource groups and cost.

mstr.name: Object Manager promotion
mstr.note: Object Manager moved selected objects and their dependencies between environments; Git, pull requests, CI and deployment pipelines now promote code and configuration.

Team topologies for data and AI
